title: Swatches!
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck discuss the history of the Swatch watch. They describe how the Swiss watch industry crisis of the 1970s-80s, caused by Japanese quartz watches such as Seiko's Astron, led Nicholas Hayek to merge two failing Swiss companies and create a cheap, stylish, Swiss-made plastic watch. Topics include the engineering (fewer parts, injection molding, Ernst Thomke, Elmar Mock, Jacques Müller), the marketing (fashion-item positioning, seasonal "drops," collaborations with artists like Keith Haring, Yoko Ono and Alexander Hofkunst, and sponsorships such as the Swatch Watch New York City Fresh Fest and Impact skateboarding tour), counterfeits, distribution in the US, product flops (phones, Swatch Beat), the Swatch Mercedes Smart car, and the company's later success. The episode ends with a request for ratings and reviews and listener contact information. Personal anecdotes from the hosts are also included.
topics: Swatch Watch New York City Fresh Fest

segments.title: Opening banter and personal swatch collections
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce swatches, share personal watch stories, Josh's honeymoon Swatch purchases, and the giant Maxi wall clock. They tease the Swatch ticking sound and the history to come.

segments.title: Swiss watch tradition and the arrival of quartz
segments.summary: They describe Switzerland's reputation for watchmaking craftsmanship and how Seiko's Astron, the first quartz watch, launched in December 1969 and disrupted the industry. They explain how quartz oscillation simplifies watches and how quartz second hands tick differently from mechanical sweep hands.

segments.title: Swiss watch industry crisis and Nicholas Hayek's merger
segments.summary: Seiko overtook Swiss makers as the top watch company by revenue, and the Swiss share of the market collapsed. Nicholas Hayek, a business consultant, proposed merging two failing Swiss companies rather than selling off their brands.

segments.title: Early designers and the thinnest watch
segments.summary: Hayek aimed to make cheap, stylish Swiss watches. Ernst Thomke, Jacques Müller and Elmar Mock contributed designs and engineering, and Thomke's Delirium was a very thin quartz watch.

segments.title: Plastic injection molding and reduced parts
segments.summary: Elmar Mock pushed for plastic injection molding, and the watch case was built to hold the movement parts, further cutting the number of parts needed.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Cheap Swiss watch strategy and fashion marketing
segments.summary: Switzerland kept production in-country and aimed for low prices through manufacturing innovation. Hayek positioned Swatch as a fashion item people would buy several of, not jewelry. The name's origin is discussed, with consultant Franz Schrepfer credited with coining it as Swiss plus Watch. The first twelve models launched in March 1983 in Switzerland, Germany and the UK in Swiss Army colors.

segments.title: Swatch drops and collectibility
segments.summary: The 1983 Jellyfish was a hit, and Swatch began releasing seasonal collections and limited one-off specials. Scarcity drove collecting.

segments.title: Eighties fashion and headbands
segments.summary: Hosts riff on eighties fashion, including Japanese-flag headbands and Chuck's party costume.

segments.title: Sponsorships, hip hop tour and watch knockoffs
segments.summary: Swatch sponsored the Swatch Watch New York City Fresh Fest in 1984, described as an early hip hop tour with Houdini, Curtis Blow, Run-DMC and the Fat Boys. Competitors such as Guess and Armitron emerged, and counterfeit Swatches flooded the market, with about ten thousand fakes imported daily in 1984 versus eleven thousand legitimate watches sold. Swatch also sponsored the Impact skateboarding tour from 1988.
topics: Swatch Watch New York City Fresh Fest

segments.title: Artist collaborations
segments.summary: Swatch collaborated with artists, including Keith Haring's four 1986 designs, which are highly collectible; Andy Warhol referred them to Haring. Yoko Ono and Pigcasso also contributed designs.

segments.title: Alexander Hofkunst food-themed Swatches
segments.summary: Hofkunst designed three 1991 food-themed Swatches (bacon and eggs, a cucumber, and a tomato) sold in European supermarkets.

segments.title: US distribution and personal watch memories
segments.summary: Swatch first tried selling through US jewelry stores in San Antonio, Texas, which did poorly, so it moved to department stores and other outlets, catching on first on the coasts. Hosts share memories of their first Swatch purchases and working as kids.

segments.title: Brunswick stew anecdote
segments.summary: Chuck recounts working as a busboy at age twelve at a barbecue restaurant, and a Brunswick stew story comes up, followed by a break.

segments.title: Other Swatch products and flops
segments.summary: Other products included the Swatch phone, Maxi clock, scented Granita de Frutta watches, the 1989 Twin phone, and the 1998 Swatch Beat, which divided the day into one thousand beats. Later Swatch made mechanical and metal watches, and a Nokia-partnered phone in 1993 did not sell well.

segments.title: Digital watches and the Smart car
segments.summary: The company made an early touchscreen watch, and it collaborated with Mercedes on the Smart car, which stood for Swatch Mercedes Art car and was originally to be called the Swatchmobile. Scott Ackerman's factoid is mentioned.

segments.title: Swatch success figures and repairability
segments.summary: Sales figures of 1.1 million watches in 1983 and 12 million a year later are given. The merged company's losses turned into profits, reaching over a billion dollars in 2023. Swatch said the watches are designed to last thirty years and cannot be repaired.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: Chuck says he is waiting for his Swatch to arrive and will post about it on Instagram.

segments.title: Listener mail replacement and ratings request
segments.summary: Instead of listener mail, the hosts ask listeners to rate and review the show and to send swatch photos to the show's email address.
